title: The Białystok Pogrom of 1906: Wounds, Witnesses, and a Community Under Attack
summary: The pogrom was a defining trauma for the community and prompted both immediate aid for victims and wider political scrutiny.
editorialContent:
![Białystok, the city at the centre of the pogrom](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg/1920px-Bazylika_w_Bia%C5%82ymstoku_-_Emilia_Ernst.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## Three days remembered

For Białystok’s Jews, the pogrom of June 1906 was not an isolated eruption of violence but a catastrophe that struck amid political repression and mounting fear. The memorial book’s accounts place the attack over three days, from June 1 to 3, 1906, and remember it as an assault on people, homes, shops, and the security of Jewish life in the city. Five overlapping records in the book describe the event and its effects: [the June 1906 pogrom]( /communities/bialystok/records/mention_8593c15541b6ba93dcfe7729), [the 1906 pogrom]( /communities/bialystok/records/mention_13899e26133ef1b07d207ab0), [the pogrom remembered by survivors]( /communities/bialystok/records/mention_9b0d4fd0cc1cb5b17eaf9fcd), [the account of the delegation and hospital]( /communities/bialystok/records/mention_5756ada1eb18a854442a3160), and [the record of killings, looting, and wounded victims]( /communities/bialystok/records/event_candidate_b81cb0fb4dc67c7a14a71125).

The dates need a calendar note. The memorial book gives June 1–3; the English-language historical record usually gives June 14–16, 1906, identifying those as the same dates in the Gregorian and Julian calendars respectively. Virtual Shtetl also dates the pogrom to June 14–16, while its community history describes the violence in the context of the Russian Revolution of 1905–06. ([Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/b/397-bialystok/99-history/137067-history-of-community); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bia%C5%82ystok_pogrom))

Białystok’s Jewish community lived amid industrial growth, political ferment, and state repression. Virtual Shtetl notes the strength of the Jewish Bund among the city’s workers and describes army and police repression before the 1906 massacre. It reports about 70 Jewish dead, six Christian dead, and at least 90 seriously wounded. Those figures differ from the memorial book’s account; neither should be made to erase the other. ([Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/b/397-bialystok/99-history/137067-history-of-community))

## The hospital and the wounded

The memorial book makes the Jewish hospital a centre of the story: a place where injured people were treated, the dead were brought, and relatives searched for those who had vanished into the violence. Its account of the [Jewish Hospital in Białystok]( /communities/bialystok/records/mention_863a8fc296b108a0d4c6c363) describes a courtyard filled with bodies and wards crowded with wounded people. The book’s translated account reports 80 bodies in the courtyard and more than 200 wounded patients; it adds that 19 of the wounded later died. A separate account in the same memorial collection recalls “stacks” of victims and gives a later total of 100 dead. The precise totals vary across these recollections; the sources agree on the hospital’s terrible burden.

The hospital had a history beyond this emergency. Virtual Shtetl dates the opening of a Jewish hospital in Białystok to 1840 and identifies Elize Halbersztam as its founder. The memorial book, in its account of the pogrom, remembers the hospital through the immediate work of caring for victims. Together, the sources show an institution that was part of the community’s infrastructure—and, in the crisis, a public witness to the scale of the attack. ([Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/b/397-bialystok/99-history/137067-history-of-community))

The book also preserves the role of communal leaders who tried to reach the authorities. Dr. Reygrodski, it says, managed to leave Białystok and send a telegram from Sokółka to deputies in the State Duma. The telegram turned local suffering into a matter of parliamentary attention. The memorial book says the delegation included [Professor Shchepkin](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_598397e60cd9841c4eabfb0f), [Colonel Arkantsev](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_50380339499e92e92a56a001), and [Advocate Yakobson](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_9be7f3d4ea5bae770d26c683). According to the book, they reached Białystok on the third day and saw the destruction and the injured at the hospital. Its account links their arrival with the end of the violence; that sequence is what the book records, rather than independent proof of a single cause for the pogrom’s cessation.

## Blame, fear, and self-defence

The memorial book connects the climate of danger to the [Białystok military garrison](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_086e4a5151f63feb131e61de) and to [Sheremetiev](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_b421af0de630fd2a88a12a2f), whom it remembers as an enemy of Jews and an organizer of the pogrom. It contrasts him with [Derkatchev](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_ce40fec42a5b44a543d0b19e), the police chief remembered as a liberal and popular figure. These are the book’s claims and characterizations; they should be read as community memory, not silently converted into a judicial finding. The account also places a [Catholic procession]( /communities/bialystok/records/mention_542fb8d6791148aa5f715082) among the events surrounding the outbreak.

The memorial book remembers Jewish self-defence groups, organized by workers’ parties, as a significant means of protecting neighbourhoods. It names Khanaykes, Piaskes, Argentina, Povtshizne, and Nay-Velt among the areas it says were spared mass killing. Virtual Shtetl situates this response in a city where the Bund had substantial working-class support. The pogrom’s aftermath therefore included not only grief and material loss, but also a sharpened sense that protection could not safely be left to the authorities. ([Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/b/397-bialystok/99-history/137067-history-of-community))

Earlier violence formed part of that fear. The memorial book recalls a 1905 military shooting in which Jews were killed in and around [Surazer Street](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_2584a8819b6e3e474e397131). It also preserves a connection beyond Białystok: a report from [Grodno](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_44dd71d387485941050939dd) described people there hearing news of the pogrom and workers setting out to help. These accounts suggest how quickly the attack became a regional concern, though they do not establish a complete picture of aid or movement between towns.

## What the aftermath could—and could not—repair

The community’s memory did not stop at the hospital. The memorial book recounts funerals and a mass grave, and a later chapter describes the pogrom’s damage to Jewish political life: the Labour Zionist regional committee, it says, was nearly destroyed, while attention shifted to self-defence and assistance for the wounded. Virtual Shtetl adds a broader outcome: pogroms in Białystok helped prompt emigration, including to New York, but did not end the arrival of Jews from nearby settlements. The account points to disruption and dispersal, but also to the persistence of Jewish life in the city. ([Virtual Shtetl](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/b/397-bialystok/99-history/137067-history-of-community))

The record remains uneven. The memorial book names witnesses and institutions, but cannot stand for every injured person, family, or survivor whose story entered another town’s records or an archive elsewhere. One useful next question is what [contemporary Duma investigation documents](research:State Duma investigation of the 1906 Białystok pogrom) add to the community’s account of the delegation and the authorities’ response.
